thread.title: Amazon's Margins: What Will They Be In 2029? - Amazon.com, Inc. (NASDAQ:AMZN)

author: Billy Duberstein
title: Amazon's Margins: What Will They Be In 2029? - Amazon.com, Inc. (NASDAQ:AMZN)
text:
In my last post, I built out Amazon's (Nasdaq: AMZN ) revenue growth and mix by product category . Now onto the trickier part of the valuation: Amazon's margins.
Amazon's margins have always been a controversial subject, drawing the ire of value investors who don't see any (and can't imagine they exist), and the joy of growth investors who marvel at the company's growing (and at times, accelerating) top line.
So, there are a few parts to my estimation of current margins, as well as the ultimate margin picture 10 years from now, which will be very consequential to our ultimate valuation. The few factors to consider are:
Segment operating margins Capitalizing R&D Capitalizing Leases For those of you who don't understand capitalizing R&D and leases, this effect will add to true operating margins, but will also increase debt and assets, which will heighten the amount of capital required to grow. So, this will lower our Sales-to-capital ratio but will increase margins, thereby giving a truer picture of what after-tax earnings the company makes on its investments.
2016 and 2017 were very large investment years for Amazon, and now that the company is stepping off the gas on fixed asset investment, we are just beginning to see hints of true profitability. The question is, how much is there to go?
Segment Operating Margins As I wrote in the revenue build-up the company's current revenue mix looks like this:
But will eventually look like this:
What are each segment's margins? Here are my current estimates of GAAP operating margins per segment:
Current Year Q3 2018 GAAP Op. Margin (est.) % Revenue TTM Op. Margin Contribution Estimated Margin Online Store 0.0% 53.90% 0 Physical Stores 2.0% 7.89% 0.0015771 Third Party 14.0% 18.13% 0.0253863 Subscription Services 1.0% 5.63% 0.0005631 AWS 31.0% 10.61% 0.0328932 Other 14.0% 3.84% 0.0053815 Operating margin (check) 6.58% Author estimates. Table by author
Again, the only one we know of is AWS. I estimated that the e-commerce ecosystem (subscription, direct sales, physical stores) operates around break-even due to international losses (although these are narrowing).
In fact, the past quarter showed some of the operating leverage inherent in the business model. The overall business had GAAP operating margins of 6.6% in Q3. AWS was 31%, but even the core North America business managed a 5.9% operating margin as international still posted an operating loss of (2.5%) -- though that is quickly narrowing.
In the trailing twelve months, Amazon has made, on a straight GAAP basis, $10.76 billion operating income on revenue of $220.957 billion, or about 4.8% operating margin.
Notice, this is well below last quarter’s operating margin of 6.6%, which means even on a GAAP basis, Amazon is rapidly leveraging its fixed cost base.
Changing operating margins over 10 years The big question in the valuation is, how will Amazon's margin profile change over the next 10 years?
It’s hard to adjust everything 10 years out, but I can make some GAAP assumptions for the amount of expansion, the apply it to my adjusted margin profile currently.
Starting with this year's segment margin assumptions:
Margin segment assumptions 2018: Online store: Breakeven
Physical stores: 2% -- Whole Foods had been a roughly 5% operating margin business before Amazon bought it, but Kroger (NYSE: KR ) is a little over 2%. Given Amazon’s penchant for cutting prices and driving sales, I estimate a compression has already happened down to 2% operating margins, bu I also suspect the business will grow over time and help add to Prime subscriptions.
Subscription Services: I also assume that subscription services is roughly breakeven, with about a 1% margin right now. I think Amazon is reinvesting all of the extra profit into Video and potential for increased postal costs. This is somewhat inconsequential as subscriptions are only 5.6% of sales over the TTM.
Third Party : 14% -- This is a total guesstimate on my part, and largely comes from what third-party needs to be given the margin profiles of the other businesses. Assuming a high-volume business, I think that looks okay.
AWS : Given - 31%
Other: 14% -- Remember this is mostly online advertising. It’s hard to exactly know how much margin there is in this business. I assume it’s relatively high, given that Google has operating margins of about 25% (even given the losses in its Other Bets segments) and Facebook (Nasdaq: FB ) has huge margins in the upper 40’s (though that is set to come down due to increased controls/safety).
Of course, Amazon’s advertising isn’t at the scale of these others, so I guesstimated a roughly 14% operating margin, but one that should expand as revenue grows strongly over the next few years.
Assumptions for 2029 margins - Segments Online store: 1% I think Amazon can probably sell 1P goods at slightly above break-even. International is still negative, but should leverage positively as it scales. It’s hard to know this exactly though.
Physical stores: 3% - This is probably conservative but I feel that Amazon will keep lowering prices to drive volume, top-line and ROIC. Amazon Go should help expand profit margins due to the cashier-less part of it, and Whole Foods may benefit from Amazon’s operational expertise over time (after all, Whole Foods used to be a 6% operating margin business! Note -- even this 3% assumption is well below Whole Foods’ old operating margin. I am forecasting pretty robust top-line growth for this business at 10% over the next few years, which fits in with Amazon's low-margin/ high turnover ethos.
Third Party : 20% I think t can expand from 14% to 20% as Amazon can raise fees (which it has been known to do) and leverage more of its fixed warehouse space.
Subscription Services: Still keeping this at 1% -- it’s only 6% of sales by 2029 by my estimates, and I sort of distributed the margin to online stores and physical stores.
AWS: Slight operating leverage to 35%. This is really the most consequential part of this whole matter, since this will likely be the highest-margin business Amazon has, and will grow from 11% of sales today to ~25% in 2029 by my estimates.
For the 35% operating margins, I look at an entrenched enterprise platform company such as Oracle (Nasdaq: ORCL ) , which actually has an operating margin of 36%. Microsoft is at 32% but is investing heavily in cloud and LinkedIn. So, I think this is an okay margin to be conservative.
Considering the AWS margin grew from 25.5% in Q3 2017 to 31% in Q3 2018, who knows what the true operating margin could be? 40%? 50%? Visa (NYSE: V ) has operating margins of 66%. Could AWS utility-like profile in an oligopoly with Microsoft and Google and now IBM (NYSE: IBM ) reach those heights?
Basically, it is really AWS that is driving much of our valuation. At 35%, I think this is actually on the conservative side of the base case, but I forecast fairly strong top-line growth over that time, as outlined in Part 1 .
Other: I assume Amazon advertising will grow a lot revenue-wise, but only expand operating margins to 20%.
The end result of these assumptions yields a 15.48% GAAP operating margin at "mature" Amazon or about 900 bps of operating margin expansion from the current adjusted EBIT margin of 11.71%.
Margin estimates - Year 10 Assuming slight margin expansion in each category over ten years, this is what I see the business looking like in 2029:
Product Segment Margin % Revenue Year 10 Contribution to margin Online Store 1.00% 31.72% 0.003171992 Physical Stores 3.00% 6.00% 0.001799787 Third Party 20.00% 22.78% 0.045561922 Subscription Services 1.00% 6.56% 0.00065612 AWS 35.00% 24.77% 0.086700245 Other 20.00% 8.17% 0.016334264 2029 GAAP Operating margin (Est.) 15.42% So, between Q3's 6.58% operating margins and the year 10 2029 15.42% GAAP operating margins, that's about 900 bps of margin expansion.
However, Amazon is and will likely be reinvesting in growth and will also carry operating leases, which means my operating margins need to be adjusted higher.
Amazon invests a ton in R&D, and also makes ample used of financial and capital leases. These need to be adjusted, which will increase operating margins but again -- will also increase debt and invested capital .
Capitalizing R&D Since Amazon is a long-term focused tech growth company, I capitalize R&D costs to garner a truer picture of Amazon's ROIC and margin profile. This is prudent for tech and biotech companies where the R&D can be thought of as a capital investment in future growth, especially for high-growth companies.
Amazon groups R&D in its “technology and content” category, which I believe also includes the Amazon Prime video content (which should already be amortized), but it’s still probably a decent proxy.
Last year, I amortized Amazon’s R&D over 7 years. That may have been aggressive, as usually a 2-5 year time frame is suggested for tech companies. However, Amazon is much more long-term oriented than other companies (most companies say they are, but it’s really just lip service -- Amazon means it).
Still, since Amazon seems to be moving into more of a profitable stage of its corporate life, I’ll dial back the R&D amortization period to 5 years.
In the past twelve months, "technology and content" grew 20% YOY. This was a deceleration of the first nine months growth of 30% YOY. and even further down from the 34.3% growth over the past 12 months.
So there appears to be some “stepping off the gas” that Amazon is doing. Keep in mind though, this is not a lowering of R&D, just lowering it as a % of revenue.
In the table below, I computed the past year’s R&D over the past 12 months. Since I didn’t want to have to go back five years and compute the TTM figure for the Q3 of the previous years, I just used the annual figures for prior years. This has the effect of slightly inflating R&D costs and makes this capitalized figure a bit conservative around the edges, although if my 5-year amortization period is aggressive, this will mute those assumptions.
As you can see, this has the effect of increasing EBIT by about $14 billion over the past twelve months, more than doubling the GAAP EBIT of $10.76 billion.
This also creates an additional asset which will affect our sales-to-capital ratio (by pushing up capital, making the business less efficient).
That will increase the need for reinvestment and, while expanding the margin, should be somewhat neutral to free cash flows because R&D will now be grouped in with regular Capex (for all of you critics out there, I suggest you read Aswath Damodaran ’s writings on this matter).
Capitalizing operating leases, along with capital and finance leases Another element to capitalize is operating leases, which will also have the effect of increasing operating margins while also increasing the company’s debt and capital ratios.
In addition, Amazon also uses a heavy amount of financial and capital leases for data centers and equipment for warehouses.
After parsing through Amazon’s financial statements, it appears the company does a lot of the work for you here, putting parts of capital and finance leases as debt instruments in the “other long-term liabilities” section.
Note 3 of the footnotes to Amazon’s latest 10Q, the company highlights:
"(1)Excluding interest, current capital lease obligations of $5.8 billion and $6.9 billion are recorded within “Accrued expenses and other” as of December 31, 2017 and September 30, 2018, and $8.4 billion and $8.7 billion are recorded within “Other long-term liabilities” as of December 31, 2017 and September 30, 2018.
(2)Excluding interest, current finance lease obligations of $282 million and $391 million are recorded within “Accrued expenses and other” as of December 31, 2017 and September 30, 2018, and $4.7 billion and $6.5 billion are recorded within “Other long-term liabilities” as of December 31, 2017 and September 30, 2018.”
Source: Amazon 10Q
So, I just added $8.7 billion in LT capital leases and $6.5 billion in LT finance leases to the company’s current $24.7 billion in book debt on the balance sheet.
I did NOT amortize these capital and finance lease payments as it appears as though Amazon already does this for you, so no added benefit to the EBIT line (these payments show up as principal payments on the cash flow statement).
Operating Leases I do have to do some work and estimation for operating leases , however:
To estimate the current TTM operating lease payments, I just took the next three months’ commitment ($748 million) and multiplied by four. It’s somewhat crude, but it's not given by the company (at least that I can find), so I had to do some guesstimation here. It shouldn't be too consequential to the overall valuation.
Also, “year 1” is just the next three months of the year as given by the company, with the next four 12 months years. This is probably not 100% accurate but probably fairly close. Since we are working with September Q3 numbers (not full-year), it’s a bit wonky.
For cost of debt, I used 4.1%, about 100 bps higher than the 10-year T Note. This comes from a rough average of bond rating spread from Fitch (A+), Moody’s (Baa1), and S&P (AA-). I happen to think the risk profile is at the low end of these, but taking an average to be somewhat conservative.
That adjustment adds another $1 billion to operating earnings, but creates another $19.5 billion in debt – this debt will be subtracted from enterprise value at the end of the valuation.
Final adjusted EBIT - Current Year My adjusted EBIT for the TTM runs at $25.87 billion, for an 11.71% "true" operating margin.
These adjustments has raised the amount for capital that will be calculated sales-to-capital ratio and ROIC as well. It has also raised the debt to be subtracted from final enterprise value from about $25 billion on the balance sheet to almost $60 billion .
These adjustments will also lower the sales-to-capital ratios. So again, for all of you yelling about this artificially inflating valuations, keep that in mind.
Sales-to-Capital Ratio Since we will be dealing with a changing margin profile in the 10 year DCF, I will use the method of using a sales-to-capital ratio in order to estimate reinvestment needs in the model.
Taking the prior adjustments to the asset base and running them through this formula:
TTM Revenue/ (This year’s debt+equity+capitalized leases+R&D Asset) – (Last year’s debt+equity+capitalized leases+R&D asset) / 2)
Sales-to-Capital = 4.25
This is the sales-to-capital ratio I’ll use here for the entire model – although it’s entirely possible that the company becomes more efficient than this as it matures (needing less capital to generate as much revenue, since much of this is fixed costs). Still, for the sake of conservatism, I’ll use 4.25.
While all you may be hemming and hawing, all of my assumptions yield a FCF margin of 6.2% in 2019. That is not very far off this past quarter’s 6.6% operating margin (after tax EBIT would be ~5% assuming a 27% tax rate) and this year’s fourth quarter should be even more profitable.
Taxes: In my model I'musing a 27% tax rate, well above the corporate tax rate due to state taxes as well as perhaps an added European tax -- this is perhaps a conservative measure.
So, next year I forecast a FCFF number of about $15.7 billion:
Year 10 Adjusted Operating margins and FCF For year 10, I merely estimate an expansion of 900 bps (estimated from my GAAP RBIT figures in year 10), but then I apply it to the current adjusted EBIT margin of 11.71%.
This would yield about a 20.71% adjusted operating margin , which I will take down to 20% for conservatism’s sake in year 10.
So my Year 10 EBIT margin assumption for Amazon is 20%
Based on my current sales-to-capital ratio and margin expansion, ROIC will increase from the current 13.85% ROIC figure. As the company scales across its fixed asset base and AWS grows and expands margins, Amazon eventually becomes a 40% ROIC business.
This is certainly not out of the realm of possibility when you consider the outsized ROICs of fellow large tech peers Apple (Nasdaq: AAPL ), Google, and Facebook, for instance (some are approaching triple-digit ROICs).
After year 10, I have kept growth of 3% (a shade below the 10-year T-note), but lowered ROICs as Amazon's competitive advantages mature and it may susceptible to new technologies.
On the other hand, if Amazon chooses to milk its assets for cash, that would result in lower terminal growth, but higher ROICs (and thus less reinvestment), making the terminal FCF number somewhat of a wash. As it stands, I have FCF declining in year 11, but growing at a terminal rate of 3%.
See the built out tables below:
Thus in year 11 (or, 2030), I estimate Amazon will generate about $80 billion in free cash flow.
Next installment, I'll calculate Amazon's cost of capital (and whether it changes), as well as adjustments for cash and debt, along with the final valuation number and sensitivity tables to key variables.
